Football – An overview of the world sport

Football is more than just a sport – it's a global language. Four billion fans worldwide, playing it in every corner of the earth. Whether in a club, in the local league, or with friends in the park: football connects people.

For players, football means 90 minutes of peak performance, thousands of decisions per game, teamwork, and individual brilliance. This guide shows you what makes the sport so special and how you can improve your performance.

What makes football special?

Simple basic rules: Ball in the goal – everyone understands that. Complex tactics: Endless variations of playing systems. Universal: Playable anywhere, minimal equipment. Team: 11 players, different roles, one goal.

Physical requirements

Modern football is high-intensity: 10-13 km covered per game. Of that, 15-25% is high-intensity (sprints). 1,000+ changes of direction per game. 150-250+ touches on the ball.

Positions and their requirements

Each position has different physical and technical profiles.

goalkeeper

The ideal position: Explosive jumping ability and quick reflexes. Good football technique (playmaking). Mental strength: One mistake can decide the game. Leadership qualities (overview, communication).

Center-back

The bulwark: aerial prowess and tackling strength. Anticipation: reading situations. Build-up play: passing from the defense. Less running, more challenges.

Full-back

The hybrids: Highest running performance of all positions. Offensive and defensive tasks. Crossing, dribbling, defensive work. Endurance and sprinting ability are required.

Defensive midfielder (number 6)

The organizer: Strength in one-on-one situations and game awareness. Tactical understanding. Passing accuracy. Less spectacular, but indispensable.

Central midfielders (8/10)

The heart of the team: Maximum ball contact. Creativity and playmaking. Box-to-box ability (number 8). Goal creation and threat (number 10).

winger

The pace-setters: speed and dribbling. One-on-one strength. Crosses or drives towards goal. Sprint endurance for repeated actions.

striker

The finishers: Goal threat and finishing ability. Movement in the penalty area. Heading crosses. Pressing and closing down (modern football).

Training for footballers

Football training is multifaceted: technique, tactics, fitness and mental strength.

Technical training

The foundation of all football: Ball control: The first touch is decisive. Passing: Short, long, with different feet. Dribbling: Keeping the ball under pressure. Shooting: Different techniques, different situations.

Tactical training

Teamwork: Game formats: 4v4, 7v7, 11v11. Position-specific: Running patterns, behavior in situations. Pressing: When and how to attack? Build-up play: Controlled forward from the goalkeeper.

Endurance training

Football-specific: Intervals: Reflect the stop-and-go nature of the game. High-intensity interval training (HIIT). Endurance base: GA1 runs during pre-season training. Game-like drills with an endurance component.

Speed ​​training

For explosive actions: Sprint training: 5-30m sprints. Agility: changes of direction, reaction time. Coordination ladder, cone drills. Explosive power: jumps, starts.

Strength training

Essential in modern football: Legs: Squats, lunges. Core: Stability for challenges. Upper body: For physical engagement. Injury prevention: Eccentric exercises for hamstrings.

The season setup

The football season has a clear structure – the training must follow.

Summer preparation

Lay the foundation: 4-6 weeks before the season starts. Build up your endurance base. Intensify strength training. Play test matches for match practice.

Season phase

Match schedule: The weekend game dictates the week. Prioritize recovery after matches. Load management: Avoid high intensity every day. Practice tactics and set pieces.

Winter break

Short recovery and build-up phase: 2-3 weeks off. Then: Rebuild phase similar to summer pre-season training (shorter). Focus on weaknesses from the first half of the season.

End of season

Decisive matches: Reduce workload. Maintain freshness and sharpness. Mental preparation for important games.

Off-season

Regeneration and individual training: 2-4 weeks of active recovery. Other sports (cross-training). Addressing individual weaknesses. Healing from injuries.

Nutrition for footballers

Proper nutrition is performance on the pitch – from preparation to recovery.

Basics

Energy requirements: 2,500-4,500 kcal/day depending on training volume. Carbohydrates for energy (50-60%). Protein for regeneration (1.5-2g/kg body weight). Fats for hormonal balance and energy storage.

Matchday

Timing and content: Last large meal: 3-4 hours before kickoff. High in carbohydrates, easily digestible. Small snack: 1-2 hours beforehand (if needed). Hydration: Start hours in advance.

Half-time

Use the short break to your advantage: drink water or an isotonic beverage. Perhaps a carbohydrate snack (gel, banana). Not too much – you don't want blood in your stomach.

After the game

Recovery window: Within 30-60 minutes: Protein + carbohydrates. Replenish fluids (1.5 times the amount lost). Electrolytes if sweating heavily.

Training week

Adaptation to training load: High training intensity: More carbohydrates. Recovery days: Moderate, more protein. Game preparation: Carb-loading the day before the game.

Injuries in football

Football carries a risk of injury – prevention is key.

Frequent injuries

Common football injuries: Muscle injuries: hamstrings, adductors, calves. Ligament injuries: cruciate ligament (ACL), ankle. Overuse injuries: groin, pubic bone, Achilles tendon. Contact injuries: contusions, fractures.

Torn cruciate ligament – ​​The dreaded injury

The worst-case scenario: 6-12 months of downtime. Often without contact (landing, change of direction). Risk factors: fatigue, landing technique. Rehabilitation is challenging.

Prevention

What helps: FIFA 11+: Prevention program (20% fewer injuries). Strength training: Especially eccentric exercises for hamstrings. Nordic hamstring curls: Gold standard. Proprioception: Balance training. Warm-up: Dynamic warm-up before every session.

Fatigue and risk of injury

Consider the connections: End of game: More injuries in minutes 75-90. Match frequency: English weeks increase the risk. Sleep and recovery: Underestimated factors.

Game systems and tactics

Football tactics are a game of chess in real time – here are the basics.

Formations

The most well-known systems: 4-3-3: Offensive, wide squad. 4-4-2: Classic, balanced. 4-2-3-1: Modern, controlled. 3-5-2: Focus on the wings, risky at the back. 5-3-2: Defensive, counter-attack-oriented.

Possession

Dominance through control: Positional play: Creating numerical superiority. Short passes: Making the opponent run. Patience: Waiting for an opening. Tiki-taka: The extreme form.

Pressing

Active ball recovery: High pressing: Disrupt the opponent early. Medium pressing: Compact midfield. Low pressing: Invite the opponent in, then attack. Counter-pressing: Attack immediately after losing possession.

Switching game

Transitions decide games: Counter-attacks: Quickly after winning the ball. Switching to defense: Securing possession after losing the ball. Transition is often the decisive moment.

Standards

Goals from set pieces: 30-40% of all goals come from set pieces. Corners, free kicks, throw-ins. Well-rehearsed routines. Defensive organization is just as important.

Mental strength in football

Football is won in the mind – mental strength makes the difference.

High-pressure situations

When it counts: Penalty kicks: Technically simple, mentally extreme. Decisive games: Playoffs, relegation battles. Comebacks from behind: Mentality vs. giving up.

Dealing with mistakes

Everyone makes mistakes – the reaction is what counts: Short memory: Focus on the next action. Don't dwell on it: Mistakes happened. Self-confidence: Show initiative anyway.

Team dynamics

Team as a unit: Communication: On and off the field. Respect hierarchy: Captain, experienced players. Resolve conflicts: Not on the field. Common goals: Over individual interests.

Visualization

Mental training: Rehearse game situations before the game. Visualize successful actions. Routine: Standardize preparation.

concentration

90 minutes of focused practice: Rituals: Fixed routines for focus. Triggers: Getting back into the game after distractions. Breathing techniques: Brief moments of calm.

Equipment for footballers

The right equipment improves performance and protects against injuries.

Football boots

The most important equipment: Studs: FG (Firm Ground) for dry grass. SG (Soft Ground) for wet grass. AG (Artificial Grass) for artificial turf. TF (Turf) for hard surfaces. Material: Leather (fit, ball feel) vs. synthetic (lightweight, water-repellent). Fit: Snug, but not constricting.

shin guards

Mandatory equipment: Size: From the ankle to below the knee. Material: Plastic, some with foam padding. Ankle protection: Optional, for added safety. Secured with socks.

clothing

Functional: Jersey and shorts: Breathable, lightweight. Baselayer: Compression, warmth in cold weather. Socks: Long enough for shin guards. Gloves: For outfield players in cold weather.

ball

Standards: Size 5 (adults), Size 4 (youth). FIFA quality for competitions. Good ball feel for training with quality balls.

Training equipment

For individual training: cones, poles, agility ladders. Rebounders for passing technique. Goal nets for shooting practice.

Getting started in football

Anyone can play football – here you'll find the perfect way to get started.

Club search

The classic approach: DFB club search: dfb.de. From district league to Bundesliga: A club for every level. Adult teams are often looking for players. Youth: Structured training from a young age.

Starting as an adult

Never too late: Hobby teams: Low level, lots of fun. Recreational leagues: Organized matches without club membership. Veterans / Over 30s / Over 40s: For older beginners. Football courses: Learn basic techniques.

Football pitch and friends

Unstructured: Kick-off in the park: Spontaneous, low barrier to entry. Small field: 5v5, 7v7 – more ball contacts. Fitness and fun without pressure.

Fitness preparation

If you haven't played for a long time: Build up your basic fitness: running, intervals. Stabilize your ankles: balance training. First ball contacts: alone or with friends. Then: join team training.

Equipment for the start

Minimal equipment: Football boots (suitable for the playing surface). Shin guards. Sports clothing. Ball for practice.

In professional football: 10-13 km per game. Full-backs and midfielders cover the most. Of this, 15-25% is high-intensity (sprints, fast running). Slightly less in lower leagues.

Primarily legs: quadriceps, hamstrings, calves, glutes. But also core for stability and changes of direction. Upper body for tackling. A complete athletic workout.

A warm-up program for injury prevention, developed by FIFA. 20 minutes of exercises for strength, balance, and plyometrics. Reduces injuries by approximately 30-50%. Yes, highly recommended!

Absolutely! Amateur teams, recreational leagues, and over-30/over-40 teams welcome beginners. Basic fitness helps, but you learn as you play. The social aspect is often more important than your skill level.

Recreational: 1-2 training sessions + 1 match. Ambitious: 3-4 training sessions + 1-2 matches. Youth performance: 4-5 training sessions + match. Professional: 5-6 training sessions + match. Don't forget recovery!

Very important in modern football! Reduces the risk of injury (especially hamstrings), improves sprints and tackling ability. 2-3 times per week during preseason, 1-2 times during the season.

FIFA 11+ warm-up. Strength training (especially eccentric for hamstrings). Take recovery seriously. Get enough sleep. Be more careful when fatigued. Listen to your body.
